cards.title: What graphic design really is — communication, not just 'decoration'
cards.takeaway: Graphic design is arranging words, images, colours, and space to send a clear message to a specific audience.
cards.body:
Good design is not about piling rainbow colours and ten fonts onto a church flyer! **Graphic design is visual problem-solving**.

Before touching Canva, Photoshop, or CorelDRAW, every great designer asks two questions:
1. **Purpose:** What action should this design make someone take?
2. **Audience:** Who is looking at it (busy market shoppers, corporate CEOs, university students)?

cards.title: The 6 core principles of design
cards.takeaway: Every strong design rests on six pillars: Purpose/Audience, Hierarchy, Contrast, Alignment, Balance, and White Space.
cards.body:
Memorise these **six core principles** — they let you diagnose and fix *any* poster, flyer, or social post:
1. **Purpose & Audience:** Who is it for, and what is the goal?
2. **Hierarchy:** What the eye sees **first, second, and third**.
3. **Contrast:** Clear visual difference (light vs. dark, big vs. small).
4. **Alignment:** Invisible lines keeping edges neat and connected.
5. **Balance:** Even visual weight across the layout.
6. **White space:** Breathing room around elements!

check.prompt: Instead of saying 'This flyer is bad because it looks ugly', how does a trained designer critique a weak flyer?

choices.text: Name the exact design principle broken (like weak hierarchy, low contrast, or zero white space) and explain how to fix it
Say 'My cousin did not like the vibe'
Count how many megabytes the PNG file takes
Add seven more fonts until it looks busy

check.hint: 'Ugly' is just personal opinion — principles like Hierarchy and Contrast tell you *why* and *how* to fix it!
check.explanation: Spot on! Naming the specific principle (hierarchy, contrast, alignment, white space) turns vague criticism into an actionable fix.

cards.title: Hierarchy — guiding the viewer's eye 1st → 2nd → 3rd
cards.takeaway: If every line is the same size and boldness, NOTHING stands out! Make the main headline biggest, key details second, fine print third.
cards.body:
Imagine a concert flyer where the event title, date, venue, and sponsor phone number are **all 18pt yellow text**. Your eye doesn't know where to look!

**Hierarchy** guides the eye in order of importance:
1. **First (Biggest / Boldest):** Main hook or title (*"PORT HARCOURT TECH EXPO"*)
2. **Second (Medium):** Date, time, and main offer (*"Sat Nov 14 · Free Entry"*)
3. **Third (Smallest):** Address, contact handle, and fine details.

check.prompt: Your friend's business flyer uses the exact same font size and colour for every single line of text. Which principle is missing?

choices.text: Visual Hierarchy (and Contrast) — make the headline larger/bolder so the eye sees 1st, 2nd, and 3rd clearly

check.hint: When everything shouts at the exact same volume, nobody hears the main message first!
check.explanation: Exactly! Varying size, weight, and contrast creates clear hierarchy so readers grasp the message in two seconds.

cards.title: Contrast & Alignment — instant readability and polish
cards.takeaway: High contrast (dark ink on pale background, or crisp white on deep navy) makes text effortless to read; alignment kills messiness.
cards.body:
Two fast fixes that rescue 80% of amateur designs:
- **Contrast:** Pale yellow text on a white background forces people to squint. Pair **dark on light** or **light on dark**!
- **Alignment:** Don't scatter boxes randomly across a page. Line headings, body text, and logos cleanly along one crisp left edge or centred axis.

cards.title: White Space — empty space is NOT 'wasted' space!
cards.takeaway: White space (empty breathing room of any colour) prevents clutter, makes luxury brands feel calm, and spotlights what matters.
cards.body:
Clients often say: *'There is still space in the corner — make the logo bigger and add five more photos!'*

Resist gently! **White space** (negative space, whatever background colour you use) gives the eye **room to breathe**. Without generous margins and padding, even good text feels cramped, cheap, and exhausting to read.

check.prompt: Why is 'white space' (empty breathing room) essential on a poster or webpage?

choices.text: It prevents visual clutter, makes text easy to read, and draws focus to the important elements
It forces every background to be pure white `#ffffff`

check.hint: Think of a neat boutique display vs. a crammed market table where nothing can be seen clearly.
check.explanation: Yes! White space (in any background colour) gives your message room to breathe and makes the whole layout look trustworthy.
